Why Is CMP needed in Semiconductor 
Manufacturing? 
CMP is essential for achieving a highly planar wafer surface, controlling film thickness, and 
enabling reliable multilayer device fabrication.
Key Purposes of CMP
1.
Surface Planarization: Removes surface topography and reduces height variations caused 
by deposition, etching, and patterning.
2. Multilayer Integration: Provides a flat surface for subsequent lithography and thin-film 
deposition in advanced semiconductor devices.
3. Improved Lithography: Minimizes focus variation and depth-of-focus (DOF) limitations, 
improving pattern resolution and overlay performance.
4. Selective Material Removal: Removes excess materials while retaining desired structures, 
such as Cu interconnects, W plugs, and shallow trench isolation (STI).
5. Film Thickness Control: Achieves uniform dielectric and metal film thickness across the 
wafer.
6. Improved Device Yield and Reliability: Reduces topography-related defects, electrical 
failures, and process variability.

Chemical Mechanical Planarization (CMP) and 
Post-CMP Cleaning 
https://www.horiba.com/ind/semiconductor/applications/chemical-mechanical-planarization-cmp/
Chemical mechanical polishing (CMP) is a powerful fabrication technique that 
uses chemical oxidation and mechanical abrasion to remove material and achieve 
very high levels of planarity.
Post-CMP Cleaning:
•
Removes abrasive particles, polishing byproducts, organic residues, and metallic 
contaminants remaining after CMP.
•
Prevents defects caused by slurry particles and contaminants adhering to wafer surfaces.
•
Ensures wafer cleanliness while minimizing scratches, watermarks, surface roughness, 
corrosion, and dielectric property changes.
CMP:
•
Combines chemical reactions (oxidation) and mechanical abrasion to achieve selective 
material removal and high surface planarity.
•
Uses specially formulated slurries containing chemicals and abrasive particles.
•
Widely applied in semiconductor manufacturing for surface planarization and device 
structure formation.

Major CMP slurry components 
CMP slurry is a liquid chemical mixture containing fine abrasive particles and chemical additives, used during 
Chemical Mechanical Planarization (CMP) to remove material from a wafer surface and achieve a highly flat, 
smooth surface. CMP slurry combines two mechanisms:
1.
Chemical action: Chemicals react with the wafer surface, forming a modified layer that is easier to remove.
2.
Mechanical action: Abrasive particles, together with the polishing pad, mechanically remove the reacted 
material.

Oxidation and Complexation in Metal CMP
Metal CMP combines chemical oxidation, complexation, and mechanical abrasion to achieve 
controlled metal removal and surface planarization.
Oxidation modifies the metal surface, complexation helps remove dissolved metal species, and 
mechanical abrasion continuously renews the surface.

Key Process Challenges
•
Excessive oxidation: May increase corrosion, pitting, and unwanted metal dissolution.
•
Excessive complexation: May increase static etch rate and cause dishing.
•
Insufficient oxidation: Can reduce removal rate and polishing efficiency.
•
Chemical balance: Oxidizers, complexants, inhibitors, and abrasives must be optimized 
together.

26 
Surface Chemistry in Dielectric CMP
Dielectric CMP relies on surface hydration, chemical bond formation, and mechanical abrasion to 
remove SiO₂ and other dielectric materials while achieving high planarization efficiency and 
selectivity.
Chemical Mechanisms of Dielectric CMP
Step 1 — Surface Hydrolysis and Hydration
Water reacts with Si–O–Si bonds on the oxide surface, forming silanol (Si–OH) groups.
Step 2 — Abrasive–Surface Interaction
Silica (SiO₂) or ceria (CeO₂) particles interact with the hydrated dielectric surface.
•
Silica: Silanol interactions and mechanical abrasion
•
Ceria: Strong chemical affinity toward SiO₂ through interfacial Ce–O–Si bonding
Step 3 — Mechanical Removal
Polishing pad pressure and relative motion facilitate removal of the chemically modified 
surface layer.

Dielectric Planarization CMP 
Oxide Surface Planarization 
Remove excess dielectric material and eliminate surface topography 
to achieve a highly planar wafer surface for subsequent lithography, 
thin-film deposition, and multilayer semiconductor fabrication.
Process Principle
•
Dielectric Deposition: Deposit SiO₂-based dielectric films (e.g., 
PECVD SiO₂, TEOS oxide, or HDP-CVD oxide) over patterned 
structures, creating surface topography.
•
CMP Planarization: Remove raised dielectric regions through 
chemical reactions and mechanical abrasion.
•
Surface Leveling: Higher regions experience greater initial material 
removal, reducing height variations across the wafer.
•
Thickness Control: Control the final dielectric thickness, within-
wafer uniformity, and surface planarity.

Key Process Challenges
•
Within-wafer non-uniformity: Variation in dielectric removal rate and final film thickness.

Pattern-dependent planarization: Different polishing rates between dense and isolated

•

•

STI CMP – Removal of Overburden Oxide 
Remove excess SiO₂ deposited during Shallow Trench Isolation (STI) fabrication while maintaining 
oxide-filled trenches and a planar wafer surface.
•
Oxide Deposition: Fill etched silicon trenches 
with SiO₂ (e.g., HDP-CVD or flowable oxide), 
leaving excess oxide above the surface. 
•
CMP Planarization: Remove the SiO₂ overburden 
using chemical reactions and mechanical 
abrasion. 
•
Selective Polishing: Use an oxide-selective 
slurry to remove SiO₂ while minimizing erosion 
of the underlying Si₃N₄ polishing stop layer. 
•
Endpoint Control: Stop polishing after oxide 
clearing, with controlled overpolishing to 
minimize residual oxide and nitride loss.

Tungsten (W) CMP — Chemical Reactions 
and Removal Mechanisms
Tungsten CMP uses controlled oxidation, surface passivation, and mechanical abrasion to remove 
W overburden during contact plug and via fabrication.
1. Main Chemical Reactions
Step 1 — Tungsten Oxidation
Hydrogen peroxide (H₂O₂) oxidizes metallic tungsten to tungsten oxide (WO₃).
Step 2 — Oxide Hydration and Dissolution
Tungsten oxide may form hydrated oxide or soluble tungstate species, depending on slurry pH.

Tungsten (W) Contact Plug CMP 
Removal of W Overburden 
Remove excess tungsten (W) and barrier/liner materials after contact or via filling, leaving 
isolated W plugs with a planar surface for subsequent semiconductor fabrication.
•
Contact/Via Formation: Etch contact holes 
through dielectric layers (SiO₂) to expose 
underlying electrical connection regions.
•
Barrier/Liner Deposition: Deposit Ti/TiN or TiN
to promote adhesion, provide contact 
functionality, and support W deposition.
•
Tungsten Deposition: Fill contact holes with W, 
typically using chemical vapor deposition (CVD), 
leaving W overburden.
•
CMP Planarization: Remove excess W and 
barrier materials while retaining W inside 
contact holes.
•
Endpoint Control: Stop polishing after clearing 
the overburden and barrier layer, minimizing W 
recess and dielectric erosion.

3. Corrosion inhibition: BTA forms a protective 
surface film, helping control unwanted 
corrosion.
4. Mechanical removal: Abrasive particles and 
pad contact remove the reacted surface 
layer.
5. Planarization: The combined action 
preferentially removes protruding regions 
under appropriate process conditions.
Chemical Mechanism of CMP

40 
Cu CMP — best case study for specialty chemicals 
Cu CMP gives you an excellent example which can clearly see the roles of individual chemical families.
A simplified mechanism is:
Cu → oxidized/passivated Cu surface → abrasive removes modiﬁed layer → fresh Cu exposed → oxidation 
repeats
Hydrogen peroxide is commonly used to oxidize Cu, while complexing agents such as glycine or citrate keep 
Cu ions soluble. BTA is widely used to inhibit excessive Cu dissolution. ScienceDirect
Example chemistry
Oxidation:
Cu Cu+/Cu2+
[H₂O₂ promotes formation of Cu oxide/hydroxide species.
Complexation: Cu2+ + nL CuLn
where L = glycine, citrate, etc.
Corrosion inhibition: Cu + BTA → Cu–BTA protective/passivation layer
The abrasive then mechanically disrupts/removes the surface layer at contact points.
This creates a useful conceptual competition:
Oxidation + complexation → removal versus Passivation/inhibition → protection
CMP performance comes from balancing the two

Cu Interconnects (BEOL) CMP
Copper Damascene Planarization 
Remove excess copper (Cu) and barrier/liner materials after damascene metallization, forming

Process Principle
•
Trench/Via Formation: Pattern and etch trenches 
and vias in dielectric layers (SiO₂ or low-k materials).
•

suitable diffusion barriers and Cu seed layers.
•

Cu, leaving excess Cu overburden.
•
Cu CMP: Remove excess Cu through controlled 
chemical oxidation, dissolution, and mechanical 
abrasion.
•
Barrier CMP: Remove exposed barrier materials (e.g., 
Ta/TaN) while minimizing dielectric loss and Cu 
recess.

Key Process Challenges
•
Cu dishing: Excessive Cu removal within wide trenches, causing recessed interconnect

Dielectric erosion: Unwanted dielectric removal, particularly in dense interconnect regions.

Residual Cu/barrier: Incomplete removal may cause electrical shorts between interconnects.
•
Surface defects: Scratches, abrasive particles, organic residues, and metallic contamination.

CMP Endpoint Detection Methods 
Optical Endpoint Detection
Monitors reflected light intensity or spectral changes to detect 
film thickness and material transitions. Common in dielectric 
CMP and compatible metal CMP applications.
Motor Current / Friction Monitoring
Detects changes in polishing friction or motor 
torque when the exposed surface material changes.
Eddy Current Monitoring
Measures changes in conductive metal film 
thickness, particularly useful for Cu CMP.

47 
Time-Based Endpoint
Uses calibrated removal rate and polishing time. Simple but sensitive to process drift and wafer-
to-wafer variations.
CMP Endpoint Detection Methods 
•
Under-polishing: Residual metal or dielectric 
overburden remains.
•
Over-polishing: Excessive dishing, erosion, and 
stop-layer loss.
•
Endpoint optimization: Combine in-situ 
detection, calibrated over-polish, and post-CMP 
metrology.
Key Process Challenges
•
Selectivity vs. removal rate: High 
removal rate must be balanced against 
stop-layer protection.
•
Endpoint accuracy: Influenced by 
pattern density, film thickness variation, 
and sensor sensitivity.
•
Wafer uniformity: Different wafer 
regions may reach endpoint at different 
times.
•
Process control: Slurry chemistry, pad 
conditioning, and polishing parameters 
must remain stable.

Key challenge: CMP combines chemical and mechanical material removal, so post-CMP cleaning 
must address both chemical residues and physically attached particles without damaging the 
underlying films.
PVA Brush Scrubbing
Uses soft, porous polyvinyl alcohol brushes and cleaning chemicals to detach slurry particles and 
residues. Widely used in single-wafer post-CMP cleaning. 
Megasonic Cleaning
Uses high-frequency acoustic energy to detach fine particles without direct brush contact. Useful 
for sensitive surfaces, although acoustic damage must be controlled.
Spray / Spin Cleaning
Uses chemical or UPW spray on a rotating wafer to rinse contaminants and residues. Often 
combined with chemical treatment and spin drying.

CMP Chemicals and Post-CMP Cleaning — Key Takeaways 
•
CMP is essential for semiconductor integration, enabling planarization of STI, 
dielectric films, W contacts, and Cu interconnects.
•
CMP slurry is a chemically engineered formulation combining abrasives, oxidizers, 
complexants, inhibitors, and other additives.
•
Different materials require different slurry chemistries to achieve controlled 
removal rates, selectivity, and defect performance.
•
Post-CMP cleaning is essential for yield and reliability, removing particles, organic 
residues, and metallic contamination while protecting sensitive films.
•
CMP performance requires integrated control of chemistry, polishing mechanics, 
cleaning, metrology, and contamination.
